title: Design functional enzymes to specification across reaction classes

concept.text: Conceptual synthesis: The innovation would let a researcher specify a chemical transformation and the required catalytic performance, then obtain an enzyme that carries out that reaction with useful activity and selectivity. Its defining ambition is breadth across mechanistically distinct reaction classes, including reactions for which no already optimized catalytic motif provides a starting point. Success would require an economical design-and-test process, with a disclosed experimental screening burden.

Conceptual synthesis: Predicting how a protein folds and designing a useful catalyst address different requirements. A folded structure describes an arrangement of atoms; a catalytic specification asks whether that arrangement enables the desired chemical transformation at an adequate rate and preferentially produces the intended outcome. Computational protein design, mechanistic chemistry and biocatalysis therefore meet in this concept, but a plausible structure alone would not demonstrate completion.

significance.text: Conditional synthesis: Reliable specification-to-enzyme design would make catalytic protein engineering substantially more programmable. Researchers could begin with a desired transformation and measurable performance requirements, expanding experimental access to catalysts beyond those available through existing enzymes or optimized motifs. The direct consequence would be a broader, more predictable ability to obtain and test useful catalysts.

Conditional synthesis: That capability could support industrial synthesis, environmental applications and medicines, but each would require further development. A catalyst that works in an experimental assay may still need process integration, suitable operating conditions and economical production. Environmental and medical uses would additionally depend on delivery, persistence, specificity and safety in their intended settings. These downstream benefits are possibilities, not demonstrated outcomes of the proposed innovation.

Interpretive synthesis: The analogy to programming is useful insofar as an explicit specification would guide construction and testing. It should not imply that every chemical reaction admits a practical enzyme solution, that performance can be guaranteed without experiments, or that demonstrations on a finite panel establish unrestricted generality. The revolutionary advance would be reliable performance across a demonstrated range of chemistries within stated practical limits.

missing_breakthrough.text: Conceptual synthesis: The missing capability is a reliable, economical route from a reaction specification to experimentally verified catalytic performance across diverse mechanisms. The central challenge is not simply producing a stable protein scaffold: the design must create an active site that supports the required chemistry and achieves the specified rate and selectivity. Cases without optimized catalytic templates are essential to the ambition because they test whether the method can establish a suitable catalytic arrangement rather than depend entirely on one already available.

Engineering synthesis: A specification-driven system would need to connect mechanistic reasoning to realizable protein designs, preserve the intended catalytic arrangement in the resulting protein, and predict which candidates will function under the specified assay conditions. It would also need to distinguish candidates that merely appear structurally plausible from those likely to satisfy catalytic requirements. These are an articulation of the proposed engineering problem; the supplied source content does not establish which barriers have been overcome or their relative difficulty.

Engineering synthesis: Practical generality also requires controlling the cost of finding successful designs. Large screening campaigns or extensive subsequent optimization could obscure how much useful performance came from the initial design method. A convincing advance therefore needs explicit accounting of computational candidate generation, experimental screening, unsuccessful designs and any optimization after initial testing. The supplied materials do not quantify an acceptable burden or define the boundary between a usable catalytic motif and an already optimized template.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies Braun, Tripp et al., “Computational enzyme design by catalytic motif scaffolding,” with an online publication date of December 3, 2025 and DOI 10.1038/s41586-025-09747-9. It attributes designed catalysts for two reaction types using catalytic arrays to that work. These bibliographic details and the two-reaction scope are retained as reported information: the supplied review could not verify them against article content.

According to the supplied review, the retained PubMed artifact contains only a cookie-access challenge, without the bibliographic record, abstract, methods or results. The source index records a 153-character, untruncated extraction retrieved on November 11, 2026. An untruncated access-challenge page is not a complete scientific document, so it cannot substantiate the reported catalytic results or establish the article’s identity and publication date. This access limitation does not show that the reported work is false.

Evidence-bounded synthesis: If confirmed, the reported work would represent progress in motif-based enzyme design. Demonstrations using catalytic arrays for two reaction types would still leave a separate question about performance across diverse mechanisms, especially where suitable motifs are unavailable. The supplied materials establish neither achievement of the broader specification-to-enzyme capability nor its field-wide absence.

Assessment limitation: No bounded freshness-search record was supplied for the review’s November 1, 2026 assessment date. The later retrieval timestamp does not supply such a search or establish the state of the field on either date. The research also reports that the publisher page could not be opened, but the review found no retained documentation of that attempt. Neither missing record supports an additional conclusion about scientific progress.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Use a blinded panel of independently selected reactions spanning mechanistically distinct classes. Before designs are submitted, specify the required activity, selectivity and operating conditions for each reaction. Include reactions lacking optimized active-site templates, and disclose how that condition is defined and checked. Independent selection would reduce selection bias, while prespecified requirements would make functional success assessable.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: Set a numerical limit on the experimental screening burden before testing, and report the complete burden alongside successes and failures. Disclose how many candidates were generated, how many were experimentally tested, and whether further optimization was needed to meet the specification. The original proposal calls for a small burden, but no numerical threshold is supplied; any adopted limit would be an evaluation choice rather than an established standard.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed practical boundary

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: Independent laboratories should reproduce catalytic performance using disclosed sequences, production procedures, assay conditions and measurement methods. Controls should distinguish the intended catalytic activity from background reactions or other assay effects. Results should include unsuccessful reaction classes and the conditions under which otherwise successful designs fail, allowing readers to assess reproducibility and practical boundaries.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility requirement

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation: Completion should mean convincing, reproducible breadth across the declared panel within the declared performance and resource limits. A finite panel cannot establish literal universality. Laboratory success would also remain distinct from readiness for an industrial process, environmental deployment or medical use, each of which would require application-specific demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed interpretation

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BIO-03, “Predict the effects of genome changes across biological contexts,” overlaps through the relationship between sequence changes and function, but asks for prediction of biological consequences rather than construction of catalysts to reaction specifications. BIO-14, “Establish causal functions for noncoding elements and poorly understood proteins,” concerns discovering what existing biological components do; BIO-05 concerns designing proteins to perform a chosen catalytic task. Insights could inform each other without making the completion criteria interchangeable.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-04, “Create an experimentally predictive virtual cell,” and BIO-10, “Observe molecular state and dynamics inside living cells at scale,” could help evaluate how designed enzymes behave in cellular settings. BIO-05 can nevertheless be demonstrated through defined catalytic assays without a whole-cell model or comprehensive cellular observation. BIO-01, “Build an autonomously reproducing cell from defined components,” could potentially use designed catalysts, but requires integrated cellular reproduction beyond the scope of enzyme design.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-08, “Make major cereal crops reliably obtain most of their nitrogen biologically,” is a possible application neighbor where catalytic engineering might contribute to a larger biological system. Producing an enzyme would not by itself establish reliable nitrogen provision in crops. BIO-15, “Deliver programmable genome editors selectively to diverse cells in the body,” shares an interest in programmable molecular tools, but selective delivery across tissues is a separate capability from catalytic design.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-02, “Demonstrate a plausible chemical transition from nonlife to evolution,” and BIO-12, “Explain how biological homochirality could emerge and persist,” overlap with questions of catalysis and chemical selectivity. Engineered enzymes might provide experimental tools, but their deliberate design would not establish a historically plausible origin-of-life pathway or explain the emergence of biological handedness. BIO-11, concerning the origin of eukaryotic cells, likewise asks for an evolutionary reconstruction rather than a general catalyst-design method.

change_log.change: Preserved BIO-05 and its original title, with the innovation framed as a capability to be demonstrated.
change_log.reason: The evidence gap does not invalidate the concept or justify changing its identity.

change_log.change: Integrated the fold-versus-function distinction, cross-mechanism ambition, motif dependence and economical screening requirement into the concept and breakthrough discussion.
change_log.reason: These details explain the scientific target and distinguish it from structural prediction or narrower motif-based design.

change_log.change: Recast the December 2025 publication details and two-reaction result as reported information that the supplied review could not verify.
change_log.reason: The retained artifact contains an access challenge rather than the article record or abstract.

change_log.change: Removed the implication that the PubMed abstract had been inspected and that general specification-driven design had been shown to be absent.
change_log.reason: Missing scientific content supports neither verified results nor a field-wide negative conclusion.

change_log.change: Qualified the reported publisher-page access failure and preserved the missing freshness-search record.
change_log.reason: The review found no documented publisher access attempt or bounded search establishing the field’s state at the assessment date.

change_log.change: Expanded the completion proposal with operational definitions, independent replication, screening accounting and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: The review identified coherent evaluation principles but unresolved definitions of small screening burden and optimized templates; finite testing demonstrates bounded breadth.

change_log.change: Separated direct catalytic-design benefits from conditional downstream applications and explained relevant roster overlaps.
change_log.reason: Useful catalysts would expand experimental access, while cellular integration, deployment and other roster objectives require distinct demonstrations.

unresolved_issues: The article’s identity, author attribution, online date, two reported reaction types and catalytic-array results remain unverified against scientific document content in the supplied materials.

The supplied evidence does not establish whether broader specification-driven enzyme design has been demonstrated elsewhere or characterize the field comprehensively as of November 1 or November 11, 2026.
The research reports a publisher-page access failure, but the supplied review found no retained documentation confirming the attempt.
An operational evaluation still needs reaction-selection rules, numerical activity and selectivity requirements, assay conditions, and a quantified experimental screening budget.
The evaluation must define optimized catalytic templates and distinguish initial design performance from gains obtained through subsequent screening or optimization.
No review recommendation was rejected; the proposed reproducibility and practical-boundary details are explicitly presented as synthesis rather than sourced standards.
